reference.source: Standard cardiology and inherited cardiac conditions references
clinicalPearls: Atrial fibrillation occurring in a familial pattern, typically at a younger age and often without the usual acquired risk factors
A positive family history is itself an established risk marker, and heritability is substantial even for common-form atrial fibrillation
Rare monogenic forms are linked to variants in ion-channel genes (for example KCNQ1, KCNA5, SCN5A) and in genes such as those affecting natriuretic peptide signalling and cardiac structure
Common-form familial atrial fibrillation is largely polygenic, reflecting many common variants at loci such as those near PITX2
Early-onset atrial fibrillation may be the first manifestation of an underlying inherited cardiomyopathy or channelopathy, warranting broader evaluation
Management follows standard atrial fibrillation principles centred on stroke-risk assessment, rate or rhythm control, and treating any underlying disorder
Family history-taking and, in selected early-onset cases, genetic evaluation can uncover a treatable inherited substrate
reference.pathophysiology: Familial atrial fibrillation encompasses a spectrum from rare single-gene disorders to common polygenic susceptibility. In monogenic forms, variants that alter atrial ion currents change the action potential and refractoriness, either shortening it to favour re-entry or otherwise destabilising atrial electrical activity, while structural gene variants alter the atrial substrate. In the far more common polygenic form, the cumulative effect of many common variants influences atrial development, electrophysiology and fibrosis, lowering the threshold for triggered activity and re-entrant circuits. Ectopic firing, frequently from the pulmonary vein region, initiates the arrhythmia, which is then sustained by an abnormal atrial substrate. The shared endpoint is disorganised atrial electrical activity with loss of coordinated contraction.
additionalDifferentials: Atrial fibrillation secondary to hypertension or valvular heart disease
Atrial fibrillation from hyperthyroidism or other systemic triggers
Inherited cardiomyopathy presenting with atrial fibrillation
Channelopathies (long QT, Brugada) with atrial involvement
Atrial flutter and other supraventricular tachycardias
additionalInvestigations: 12-lead ECG and ambulatory monitoring to document the arrhythmia and its burden
Echocardiography to assess atrial size and exclude structural or valvular disease
Thyroid function tests and screening for reversible triggers
Cardiac MRI where an inherited cardiomyopathy is suspected
Genetic testing in selected very early-onset or strongly familial cases
Family history documentation and cascade evaluation where a monogenic cause is found
redFlags: Atrial fibrillation at a strikingly young age without acquired risk factors
Associated syncope or features suggesting a channelopathy or cardiomyopathy
Family history of sudden death or inherited heart disease
Rapid ventricular rates causing haemodynamic compromise
reference.prognosis: Prognosis largely reflects the thromboembolic risk and any underlying structural or electrical heart disease; with appropriate anticoagulation decisions and rhythm or rate control, outcomes are generally favourable, though recurrence is common and an identified inherited substrate may carry additional implications.
pitfalls: Overlooking a family history that reframes early-onset atrial fibrillation as inherited
Missing an underlying cardiomyopathy or channelopathy heralded by the arrhythmia
Assuming a monogenic cause when most familial cases are polygenic
Neglecting stroke-risk assessment because the patient is young
references: ESC guidelines on the management of atrial fibrillation
management: Assess thromboembolic risk and offer oral anticoagulation, preferring a direct oral anticoagulant, to eligible patients for stroke prevention
Rate control with a beta-blocker or other rate-limiting agent to relieve symptomatic burden
Rhythm control with antiarrhythmic drugs and/or pulmonary vein isolation by catheter ablation, particularly valuable in younger early-onset patients
Identify and treat reversible triggers and contributors, including thyroid dysfunction and obstructive sleep apnoea
Risk-factor modification with weight optimisation, alcohol reduction and blood-pressure control
Evaluate for and manage an underlying inherited cardiomyopathy or channelopathy where early-onset disease raises suspicion
Genetic counselling and cascade clinical evaluation of relatives where a monogenic cause is identified
